a.text: 1) The "Unicorn Tapestries" (circa 1495) are shown in the Metropolitan Museum of Art.
2) The bandoneon is a wind instrument.
3) In winter the Gray Whale swims to its mating grounds.
4) The ancient Egyptian god Sobek was depicted in the shape of a crocodile.
5) The poet C. Dickens wrote the play Miss Sara Sampson.
6) The sirocco is a hot, dry wind in the Mediterranean.
7) In the 80s a food scandal took place in India with about 1,500 deaths.
8) In 1938 the British car maker Aston Martin introduced the first all-wheel-drive road vehicle.
9) The Pavane is an Italian dance from the 16th century.
10) John Knowles wrote the coming-of-age novel "A Separate Peace".
11) The Naab flows into the Danube.
12) The Carolina Wolf is a spider which lives all over North America.
13) Jack Pickford played the supporting role in Rupert Julian's film "The Phantom of the Opera".
14) The longest tunnel in the world is in Japan and 54 km long.
15) The oldest university in the world was founded in Toulouse.
16) Very few people live in the Republic of Nauru.
17) The novelist Herman Melville wrote the poem The Snow Man.
18) Lake Superior in North America is the largest lake on earth.
19) Hamburg is the European record holder for number of bridges.
20) The Bermuda Agreement was completed by the United States in 1946.
21) Compounds of nitrogen with gases are called nitrites.
22) In winter the Central European Grasshopper Warbler flies to warmer regions.
23) In the Council of the District of Columbia, most of the seats are occupied by Democrats.
24) The first electric locomotive was developed in 1897 by Werner von Siemens.
25) Locals call the golden jackal native to the jungles and mountain forests of Java and Borneo "Wau-Wau".
26) Coniferous trees grew for the first time in the Permian geological era.
27) The European adder is a snake which lives up to the polar circle.
28) The pathogens of sleeping sickness, single-celled flagella, are transmitted through the Aedes aegypti mosquito.
29) The eyes of parrots are about three times better at night than those of humans.
30) The Finn Dinghy is a one-man sport boat.
31) Boris Karloff played the lead part in Friedrich Wilhelm Murnau's "Nosferatu" film.
32) Anton Karas wrote the zither theme score for "The Third Man".
33) G Haythorn from the United States is the 1969 Pulitzer Prize winner for best original novel.
34) The Portuguese seafarer Fernando Magellan discovered the Hawaiian Islands.
35) The Prussian King Augustus I the Strong was also known as the "Soldier King".
36) If you buy stocks on one stock exchange and sell for more on another, you have made "arbitrage".
37) The Mercalli scale is an earthquake scale based on the extent of the destruction.
38) The strait connecting the Marmara Sea with the Mediterranean is the Dardanelles.
39) "The White Ring" is an association for the support of single mothers in existence since 1975.
40) The oldest museum in the world is located in Lima.
41) A caryatid carries or supports a truss in place of a pillar.
42) Joseph Beuys extensively painted action paintings, in which the process of painting creates the image content.
43) The Cuban composer Esteban Salas y Castro was also known as the "Santiago Angel".
44) The peace treaty which brought the German-French war to an end was concluded in Frankfurt.
45) In his pictures, Carl Spitzweg humorously depicts scenes from the lives of petit bourgeois and misfits in the period of Biedermeier and the Restoration.
46) The "Madonna of the Carnation" (circa 1475) is exhibited in the Alte Pinakothek in Munich.
47) Astronomers named a system of seven Earth-size planets "Trappist 1".
48) The hit song "Lili Marleen" comes from the singer and actress Hildegard Knef.
49) An unevenly matched relationship, such as an unequal or mismatched marriage is named a "misalliance."
50) An expression formed by repetition of words of the same meaning is an oxymoron.
51) Linguists constructed Ibo as an artificial language like Esperanto.
52) Ronald C. Williams built the first lawnmower in 1852.
53) Physicists call the ratio of emitted light to incidental light from a diffusely reflective surface the "albedo".
54) In philosophy something unsolvable or difficult to decide is called "enigmatic".
55) You can often enter a Gloriette (a mostly open pavilion or round temple) on a hill in baroque or classical parks.
56) The most dangerous poison for humans is the Wandering Spider's, which is native to South America.
57) The Dhana desert is located in Saudi Arabia.
58) Our Earth's atmosphere contains less than 0.001% ozone.
59) The hottest place in the world is Duri (Somalia) with temperatures averaging 34.4 ° C.
60) Etesian winds blow in Egypt, especially between May and July.
61) T. Svedberg from Sweden is the 1964 Nobel Laureate in Chemistry.
62) In 1984, a chemical disaster took place in Bhopal, India, which claimed 20,000 deaths.
63) People get sick with the Lassa fever through the filovirus, which can be passed on from person to person.
64) The chinook is a westerly wind in the Rocky Mountains.
65) The longest and heaviest crocodile is the Saltwater crocodile, which can grow up to 8m and can weigh up to 700kg.
66) The song "Blue Champagne" comes from the bandleader and songwriter Sammy Kaye.
67) The strait combining the San Pablo Bay with Suisun Bay is the Carquinez.
68) The Roe River goes to the Missouri River.
69) John Collier exclusively sculpted found objects using scrap industrial metal to create sculptures.
70) In the 1600s, the Psalms were sung to the music the "Low Dutch Tune".

34) If you buy stocks on one stock exchange and sell for more on another, you have made "arbitrage".
35) The Mercalli scale is an earthquake scale based on the extent of the destruction.
36) The strait connecting the Marmara Sea with the Mediterranean is the Dardanelles.
37) "The White Ring" is an association for the support of single mothers in existence since 1975.
38) The UK's shortest canal flows through Cheshire.
39) A caryatid carries or supports a truss in place of a pillar.
40) Joseph Beuys extensively painted action paintings, in which the process of painting creates the image content.
41) The peace treaty which brought the German-French war to an end was signed in Frankfurt.
42) In his pictures, Carl Spitzweg humorously depicts scenes from the lives of petit bourgeois and misfits in the period of Biedermeier and the Restoration.
43) The "Madonna of the Carnation" (circa 1475) is exhibited in the Alte Pinakothek in Munich.
44) The hit song "Lili Marleen" comes from the singer and actress Hildegard Knef.
45) An unevenly matched relationship, such as an unequal or mismatched marriage is named a "misalliance."
46) An expression formed by repetition of words of the same meaning is an oxymoron.
47) Linguists constructed Ibo as an artificial language like Esperanto.
48) The ratio of emitted light to incidental light from a diffusely reflecting surface is the "albedo".
49) In philosophy something unsolvable or difficult to decide is called "enigmatic".
50) You can often enter a Gloriette (a mostly open pavilion or round temple) on a hill in baroque or classical parks.
51) The most dangerous poison for humans is the Wandering Spider's, which is native to South America.
52) The Dhana desert is located in Saudi Arabia.
53) Our Earth's atmosphere contains less than 0.001% ozone.
54) The hottest place in the world is Duri (Somalia) with temperatures averaging 34.4 ° C.
55) Etesian winds blow in Egypt, especially between May and July.
56) In London you can count the largest number of surveillance cameras in Europe.
57) T. Svedberg from Sweden accepted the 1964 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
58) In 1984, a chemical disaster took place in Bhopal, India, which claimed 20,000 deaths.
59) People get sick with the Lassa fever through the filovirus, which can be passed on from person to person.
60) The longest and heaviest crocodile is the Saltwater crocodile, which can grow up to 8m and can weigh up to 700kg.

b.text: 1) The Statute of Westminster was signed by the United Kingdom in 1931.
2) The bandoneon is played by blowing into it.
3) People nicknamed Henry VIII's sixth wife "Katherine the Lucky".
4) The ancient Egyptians drew the god Sobek in the form of a crocodile.
5) The play Miss Sara Sampson is by the poet C. Dickens.
6) The singer and actress Helen Shapiro sang the hit song "Honey Hush".
7) The sirocco blows hot and dry over the Mediterranean Sea.
8) In the 80s, around 1,500 people died in India, as poisoned food had entered the market.
9) The all-wheel drive was developed in 1938 by the English carmaker Aston Martin.
10) In the 16th century, the Pavane was danced in Italy.
11) The Naab flows into the Danube.
12) John Collier is considered the most important exponent of found objects, in which sculptures use scrap industrial metal.
13) The longest tunnel in the world extends over 54 km in Japan.
14) The oldest university in the world is located in Toulouse.
15) Very few people live in the Republic of Nauru.
16) The largest amount of freshwater on earth is in Lake Superior, North America.
17) Hamburg is the European record holder for number of bridges.
18) Compounds of nitrogens with gases are called nitrites.
19) In winter the Central European Grasshopper Warbler flies to warmer regions.
20) Labour is the largest party in the Durham Council.
21) Werner von Siemens built the first electric locomotive in 1897.
22) The golden jackal native to the jungles and mountain forests of Java and Borneo is also known as "Wau-Wau".
23) Conifers appeared for the first time in the Permian geological era.
24) The European adder is a snake which is widespread up to the polar circle.
25) G. Haythorn from England is the 1969 Man Booker prize winner for best original novel.
26) The 1428 sculpture "The Ascension Relief" hangs in the Victoria and Albert Museum in London.
27) The pathogens of sleeping sickness, single-celled flagella, pass through Aedes aegypti mosquito bites into the bloodstream.
28) Parrots see about three times more detail than humans at night.
29) The Finn Dinghy is a one-man sport boat.
30) Boris Karloff played the lead part in Friedrich Wilhelm Murnau's "Nosferatu" film.
31) The zither theme score for "The Third Man" is by Anton Karas.
32) The Portuguese seafarer Fernando Magellan is the discoverer of the Hawaiian Islands.
33) People also called the Prussian King Augustus I the Strong the "Soldier King".
34) The exploitation of price differences of shares traded on different stock exchanges is called "arbitrage".
35) The Mercalli scale is an earthquake scale whose values one calculates based on the extent of the destruction.
36) The Dardanelles connect the Sea of Marmara with the Mediterranean Sea.
37) In order to support single mothers, the association "The White Ring" was founded in 1975.
38) The UK's shortest canal is in Cheshire.
39) A figure holding a truss in place of a pillar is a caryatid.
40) Joseph Beuys is considered the most important exponent of action painting, in which the process of painting creates the image content.
41) The peace treaty which brought the German-French war to an end was concluded in Frankfurt.
42) Scenes from the lives of petit bourgeois and misfits in the period of Biedermeier and the Restoration are shown in pictures by Carl Spitzweg.
43) The 1475 painting "Madonna of the Carnation" hangs in the Alte Pinakothek in Munich.
44) The singer and actress Hildegard Knef sang the hit song "Lili Marleen".
45) An unevenly matched relationship, such as an unequal or mismatched marriage is a "misalliance."
46) Linguists call an expression formed by repetition of words of the same meaning an oxymoron.
47) Ibo, like Esperanto, is an artificial language.
48) Physicists call the ratio of emitted light to incidental light from a diffusely reflective surface the "albedo".
49) By "enigmatic" philosophers mean something insoluble or difficult to decide.
50) A Gloriette is a mostly open pavilion or round temple on a hill in baroque or classical parks.
51) Of all poisons, the poison of the Wandering Spider native to South America kills humans most effectively.
52) The Dhana desert is under the constitutional law of Saudi Arabia.
53) Only a very small part of the earth's atmosphere consists of ozone.
54) In Duri (Somalia), the hottest place in the world, people have to endure temperatures averaging 34.4 ° C.
55) Etesian winds occur in Egypt, especially in early summer.
56) London is the European record holder for number of surveillance cameras.
57) T. Svedberg from Sweden is the 1964 Nobel Laureate in Chemistry.
58) In 1984, a toxic gas cloud from a chemical plant in Bhopal, India, killed over 20,000 people.
59) The Lassa fever is brought on by the filovirus and can be transmitted by humans.
60) With a length of up to 8m and a weight of up to 700kg, the Saltwater crocodile is the longest and heaviest crocodile.

text.text: DEBRIEF Thank you very much for your participation. This study looks at how people make decisions about whether information is true, even if they do not know the answer. In the questionnaire you completed half of the statements were true and half were false. The statements were deliberately obscure, and we did not expect you to know the answers. We are testing the hypothesis that statements written using “concrete” words will be perceived as more likely to be true than statements written using more “abstract” words because the more concrete wording feels true. For example, people may perceive the statement, “The poet C. Dickens wrote the play Miss Sara Sampson," to be more likely to be true than the statement, “The play Miss Sara Sampson is by the poet C. Dickens.” Thank you again for participating.
